I could not find a feasible placement/path. Reasoning:

- The chain requires a path source(v2) -> f1 -> f2 -> f3 -> f4 -> f5 -> destination(v4) with each consecutive pair connected by a direct link and all VNF hosts distinct.
- That implies f5 must be a neighbor of v4 (so f5 ∈ {v2, v5}).
  - If f5 = v5, any path from v2 to v5 must go via v4 (v2->v4->v5), which would place the destination v4 in the middle of the chain (not allowed — destination must be last).
  - If f5 = v2 (i.e., last VNF on the source), then the chain must start at v2, go through 4 distinct intermediate VNF nodes, return to v2 as f5, then go to v4. That requires at least two distinct neighbors of v2 to serve as different VNF positions in the chain (one immediately after source, one immediately before returning to v2). v2's neighbors are only {v1, v4, v6}; v4 is the destination (cannot be used in middle), and v6 is a dead end (only neighbor v2). Any route that tries to connect v1 and v6 without passing through v2 is impossible, so you cannot form the required sequence of 5 distinct VNF-hosting nodes that returns to v2.
- Exploring other branches (v1->v0->v3->v10 etc.) also leads to dead ends or would require revisiting nodes or visiting the destination earlier; there is no simple walk of adjacent distinct nodes of length 6 edges from v2 to v4 that hosts five distinct VNFs.
- Link bandwidths and node CPU capacities are not the limiting factors here; the topology does not permit the required ordered sequence of five distinct VNF nodes between v2 and v4.

Therefore the VNF chain with five distinct VNFs cannot be placed respecting the path order and topology constraints; no feasible placement/path exists.
